title: The Psychology of Habits
description: Four recordings about habits: a lecture, a radio interview with a psychologist, two students talking about phones and a podcast about small steps.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · A lecture on habits
parts.intro: You will hear part of a lecture by Dr Moore about how habits work.

script.speaker: Dr Moore
script.text: Good morning. Let me begin with a surprising statistic. Researchers estimate that around forty per cent of what we do each day isn't a conscious decision at all. It's habit.

script.speaker: Dr Moore
script.text: A habit forms through a simple loop with three parts. First, a cue, which is a trigger such as a time of day, a place, or an emotion. Second, a routine, which is the behaviour itself. Third, a reward, which tells the brain that the loop is worth remembering.

script.speaker: Dr Moore
script.text: Take a very ordinary example: checking your phone. The cue might be a moment of boredom, the routine is picking up the phone, and the reward is a small burst of novelty. Repeat it enough times and the whole thing happens without thought.

script.speaker: Dr Moore
script.text: Why does the brain work this way? The answer is efficiency. Thinking is expensive in energy terms, so the brain turns repeated actions into automatic ones, freeing attention for new problems. That's why you can drive home and barely remember the journey.

script.speaker: Dr Moore
script.text: A common belief is that it takes twenty-one days to form a habit. That figure has no scientific basis. One well-known study found that the average was about sixty-six days, but with huge variation, from eighteen days to more than eight months, depending on the person and the behaviour.

script.speaker: Dr Moore
script.text: The practical lesson is to be patient, and not to give up after missing a day. Missing once made almost no difference in the long run. What matters is returning to the routine.

parts.title: Part 2 · A radio interview
parts.intro: You will hear a presenter, Daniel, interviewing a psychologist, Sofia, about breaking bad habits.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: My guest today is Sofia, a psychologist who has spent ten years studying how people change their habits. Sofia, why is it so hard to break a bad habit?

script.speaker: Sofia
script.text: Because we usually try to rely on willpower, and willpower is a limited resource. By the evening, after a day of decisions, it's nearly empty. That's exactly when people reach for snacks or the television.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: So what works better?

script.speaker: Sofia
script.text: Changing the environment. If you want to eat fewer biscuits, don't keep them in the house. It sounds almost too simple, but it removes the cue. In one study, office workers who moved sweets from the desk to a drawer two metres away ate about a third less.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Just two metres?

script.speaker: Sofia
script.text: Just two metres. A small amount of effort is often enough to break the loop.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: What about replacing a habit rather than removing it?

script.speaker: Sofia
script.text: That's the second strategy, and it's even better. You keep the same cue and the same reward, but change the routine. If stress makes you smoke, perhaps a five-minute walk gives you a similar sense of relief.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Some people say that habits are tied to personality, that you either have discipline or you don't.

script.speaker: Sofia
script.text: I'd disagree strongly. People who seem disciplined have usually just arranged their lives so that good choices are easy. It's design, not character.

parts.title: Part 3 · Two students
parts.intro: You will hear two students, Hana and Nam, talking about their phones.

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: Nam, you've been looking at your phone for the whole of lunch. We've said about ten words to each other.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Sorry. It's a terrible habit. I picked it up between lectures, and now I check it every few minutes without thinking.

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: My screen time report says I average five hours a day. I nearly fell off my chair when I saw it.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Five? Mine is closer to six and a half. I want to cut it, but every time I try, I last about a day.

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: Have you tried deleting the apps?

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: I can't delete the messaging one, because my group project depends on it.

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: Then move it. Put it in a folder on the last screen, so you have to search for it. It's a small obstacle, but it makes you think before you open it.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: That's clever. What do you do when you're bored?

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: I keep a paperback in my bag. Whenever I'd normally reach for the phone, I open the book instead. It's the same moment, but a different routine. After a month, I read three novels without really trying.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Three novels? That's more than I read all last year.

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: And I charge my phone in the kitchen overnight, so I don't scroll in bed.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Fine, I'll try the folder trick and the kitchen charging. But the paperback, I'll have to think about. I don't actually own one.

script.speaker: Hana
script.text: You can borrow one of mine. Start with something short.

parts.title: Part 4 · A podcast about small steps
parts.intro: You will hear Kevin, the presenter of a podcast, talking about starting new habits.

script.speaker: Kevin
script.text: Hello and welcome back to Small Steps. Today I'm talking about the biggest mistake people make with new habits: starting far too big.

script.speaker: Kevin
script.text: In January, a friend of mine decided to run five kilometres every morning, having not run for years. By the second week he was exhausted, by the third he had a sore knee, and by February he'd stopped completely. Sound familiar?

script.speaker: Kevin
script.text: The alternative is to make the habit so small that it feels almost silly. Instead of running five kilometres, put on your running shoes and step outside. That's it. Most days you'll end up running, but even if you don't, you've kept the habit alive.

script.speaker: Kevin
script.text: The second idea is habit stacking. You attach the new behaviour to something you already do automatically. For example, after I pour my morning coffee, I write one sentence in my journal. The coffee is the cue, so I don't have to remember anything.

script.speaker: Kevin
script.text: Third, track your progress. I use a paper calendar on my fridge and cross off each day. After a week, I don't want to break the chain. It's surprising how motivating a row of crosses can be.

script.speaker: Kevin
script.text: Finally, be kind to yourself. Everyone misses days. The people who succeed aren't those who never slip, but those who restart the next morning without a long speech of self-criticism.

script.speaker: Kevin
script.text: So, this week, pick one tiny habit, attach it to something you already do, and tell me how it goes. I'll see you next time.

questions.text: What is the lecture mainly about?
options: How to stop smoking and other bad habits
The history of psychology and the brain
How habits form and why we rely on them
Why people forget names and faces
questions.explanation: She opens with how much of our behaviour is habit, then explains the habit loop and why the brain uses it.

evidence.quote: isn't a conscious decision at all

questions.text: What is a cue?
options: A trigger such as a time or place
The pleasant feeling after the behaviour
The behaviour itself, like checking a phone
A type of memory stored in the brain
questions.explanation: The cue is the trigger that starts the habit loop.

evidence.quote: a trigger such as a time of day, a place, or an emotion

questions.text: Why does the brain create habits?
options: To save energy and free up attention
Because it cannot remember things for long
Because it dislikes rewards and new problems
To stop us feeling bored all day
questions.explanation: She says the answer is efficiency: thinking is expensive, so repeated actions become automatic.

evidence.quote: The answer is efficiency.

questions.text: What did the well-known study find about forming a habit?
options: The average was about eight months for adults
It usually took only a week or two
It always took exactly twenty-one days for everyone
About sixty-six days on average, with big differences
questions.explanation: Twenty-one days is a myth. The study found an average of sixty-six days with huge variation.

evidence.quote: the average was about sixty-six days

questions.text: What does the lecturer say about missing a day?
options: It ruins everything you have built so far
It is a clear sign of failure
It makes little difference in the end
It means starting again at day one
questions.explanation: She says missing once made almost no difference in the long run.

evidence.quote: almost no difference in the long run

questions.text: According to Sofia, why is it hard to break a bad habit?
options: People rely on willpower, which is limited
Bad habits are inherited from our parents
People never notice the cue at all
People are naturally lazy in the evening
questions.explanation: She says we rely on willpower, which is a limited resource and nearly empty by the evening.

evidence.quote: willpower is a limited resource

questions.text: What happened in the office study?
options: Workers ate about a third fewer sweets
Workers ate the same amount
Workers ate more sweets
Workers ate about half as many sweets
questions.explanation: When sweets were moved two metres away, workers ate about a third less.

evidence.quote: ate about a third less

questions.text: What is the second strategy Sofia describes?
options: Telling friends so they can help her
Removing the reward altogether from the loop
Keeping cue and reward, changing the routine
Using much stronger willpower in the evening
questions.explanation: She says you keep the same cue and reward but change the routine.

evidence.quote: You keep the same cue and the same reward, but change the routine.

questions.text: What does Sofia think about the idea that discipline is a personality trait?
options: She disagrees: it is design, not character
She agrees that some people lack discipline
She says it depends on age and family
She says nobody really knows yet
questions.explanation: She disagrees strongly: it is design, not character.

evidence.quote: It's design, not character.

questions.text: Why does Sofia mention the two-metre sweets study?
options: To show a small obstacle can break a loop
To criticise how office workers eat at their desks
To prove that sweets are cheap in offices
To advertise healthy snacks for the workplace
questions.explanation: She uses it to show that a small amount of effort is often enough to break the loop.

evidence.quote: A small amount of effort is often enough to break the loop.

options: She needs help with her group project
Nam has been on his phone all lunch
She wants to borrow his phone to call
She is angry at being kept waiting here

Starting too late in the year
